src/data/maps/bc_bellring.js.s:
THE BELLRING — CUPS TODAY
COPPER · SILVER · GOLD · SUNSTEEL
Champion: VALKA THE UNDEFEATED (41–0)
The management patches all contenders. The management is not liable for pride.
I've seen Valka fight forty-one times.
I've lost money forty-one times. I keep betting against her. It's a principle now.
When the bell rings, the whole city stops. Even the Cathedral bells wait for ours.
Don't tell the Choir I said that.
The Iron Bull was cast from a cracked bell. If you hit it right, it still rings.
Kell the Net and Kell the Fist are brothers. Kell the Third sells the pies.
The pies are the most dangerous thing here.
Between rounds we give you back a quarter of your strength. Any more and Mr. Brass says it isn't sport.
Lose a cup and we patch everything. Free. It's the only free thing in Aurenne.

src/data/maps/ch10_evernoon.js.s: Honey-buns! Fresh from the oven! Still warm — they're always still warm!
...She said that exact same thing. *Exactly* the same.
Same pitch. Same breath in the same place.
Honey-buns! Fresh from the— fresh from the— Still warm. Still warm. Still warm.
Look how high it goes! Mama, look! Look how high it goes!
There isn't a kite. He's holding nothing.
Yes, love. Very high.
She's not looking at him. She's looking at the wrong bit of sky. Forty years, the wrong bit of sky.
And-a-one, and-a-two, and-a—
Play it! Just *play* it!
And-a-one, and-a-two, and-a-one, and-a-two, and-a-one, and-a-two, and-a—
_(her bow hovers a hair above the strings, trembling, waiting for the count)_
The Lantern's humming oddly. I'll look at it after the festival. There's always time after the festival.
He doesn't know. He'll never know. He'll never get to tonight.
The Keeper says it's probably the heat. Probably the heat. It's a very hot day.
You're the Gloam! You have to catch us before the sun goes down!
...I played this. In the window. Every day.
But the sun never goes down! Ha ha! The sun never goes down!
Don't laugh like that. Don't— just don't.
Your future, dear? Oh — there isn't one. Isn't that wonderful?
She looked at me. She actually *looked* at me.
You're not from today, are you. Sister Mercy knows you're here. She knew before you did.
Some day I'll be a knight. A real one. The kind that doesn't run.
That's him. That's Sir Aldous. He's— he's younger than *me*.
Some day I'll be a knight. A real one. The kind that doesn't run.
You will be. You were. You were the best one.
_(quietly)_ And you ran, once. Back for me. That's the only running you ever did.
Some day I'll be a knight. A real one. The kind that doesn't run.
Have you seen my Lysa? She was just here. She's wearing her festival dress — white and gold, with a ribbon.
...She asks every hour. I used to answer her.
Have you seen my— have you seen— she was just here. She was just here. She was just here.
Lovely day for it!
For *what*, friend?
...Yeah. That's what I figured.
Lovely day for— lovely day for— lovely day for—
Welcome to the Festival of the Long Light. Enjoy the day.
Enjoy the day. Enjoy the day. Enjoy the day.
The fountain. Its water arcs up and hangs at the top of the arc, glittering, and does not come down.
Trays of honey-buns, glazed and golden. They are warm. They have been warm for forty years.
Nobody has ever eaten one.
The Cathedral doors are painted on. There is no inside. He never went in that day.
The Grand Lantern, humming oddly in the heat. Its light is the color of honey. It will fail tonight. It never gets to.
A cherry tree in full bloom. Petals fall from it constantly, turning in the air — and never land.
The river doesn't flow. It glitters in place, every ripple exactly where it was.
The vanity. A hairbrush with long black hairs in it, and a jar of ribbons, white and gold.
Lysa's bed. Under the pillow, a list in a child's hand: THINGS TO DO WHEN I AM GROWN UP. The list is very long.
Picture books. One is open to a drawing of an animal with a glossy black coat. Under it, in careful letters: SABLE.
A shelf of paper stars, each with a wish written inside. Most of them are about fireworks.

src/data/maps/ch10_spire.js.s: You came out. Nobody comes out.
...Was he there? A boy, nine, with a gap in his teeth? Tam. His name is Tam.
No. Don't tell me. I've decided I'm going home.
My boy is in there. Tam. He was nine.
The Choir says when the Hierophant's work is done the gate will open, and I'll see him at the festival. I've been waiting since the spring.
Is it still spring? I've lost count. Nothing changes up here. That's the point, they say.
Eleven months I've sat here. My Marigold is inside. Forty-one years married.
Some nights I can hear her laughing, through the wall. Same laugh. Same moment. Over and over.
I tell myself that's a comfort.
They say inside it's always the best day of your life. Isn't that what we all want? Isn't that what everyone has ever wanted?
I wanted my patients to get better. "Better" means "different." It means tomorrow.
...You sound very tired.
I am. That's how I know I'm still alive.
You beat the Lift-Warden? He took my slingshot once. Did you get it back? ...No? Well. Still.
The big gate never opens. Don't bother knocking; I knocked for a week.
But the white ships bring crates round the east side of the plaza. There's a lift. A man with a spear stands by it and says "halt" a lot.
Supply line
The great gate of the Spire is sealed with gold. Carved over it, in letters as tall as Pip:
AND THE GOOD DAY SHALL NOT END.
A statue of the Hierophant, arms open, smiling. Someone has left a child's shoe at its feet. Then another. Then hundreds.
A statue of a little girl in a festival dress, holding a ribbon. There is no name on the plinth.
The pilgrims' fire. Nobody needs it for warmth up here. They keep it lit so there is something that changes.
The lift's guarded.
Clock-cases, floor to ceiling. Each face is painted with the same summer sky. Each one has stopped at noon.
A clock with a child's drawing tucked into its glass: a girl, a boy, a big yellow sun, and the word ALWAYS.
The Noon Gate. Warm air breathes through it, smelling of honey and cut grass.
Not back. Never back. East — the balcony.
Lift shaft's full of light! East, sparrow — the balcony!

src/data/maps/ch11_halcyon.js.s:
THE HALCYON — Capt. C. Ashe.
Gangplank. Mind the gap. The gap is the whole sky.
The bow cuts through cloud the color of a bruise. Below: nothing at all, for a very long way.
The mainmast. Someone has carved PIP into it at a height that suggests standing on a barrel. Below it, smaller: CORVIN SAYS NO.
The foremast. A patched sail, a patched patch, and a single kite tangled in the rigging.
Corvin's chart table. Under the charts, a small painting of a woman in a Dawnguard sky-wing coat, laughing at whoever held the brush. On the back: "H.M. — don't you DARE frame this." It is framed.
Corvin's books: "Navigation for the Reluctant," "Debts and How to Outlive Them," and a much-read book of children's bedtime stories with the price still on it.
Ilse's stove. Something is simmering. It smells like home, if home were mostly onions.
Ilse's shelf: bandages rolled tight, tinctures labeled in tiny exact handwriting. One jar just says: PIP. NO.
Nell's forge, built into the ship's boiler. It runs on coal, spite and, lately, the heat of a Sun Shard on a long chain.

src/data/maps/ch11_remnants.js.s:
THE KEEPER'S HOURS
The sun wakes in the east. At noon it stands above us. At evening it goes home to the west.
Ring the hours as the sun walks them, and the Lantern will hear you.

src/data/maps/ch11_rites.js.s: ${prefix}_${spot}
c11_rite_${who}_done
A Choir supply barge, sunk with its cargo: thousands of candles, still in their wrappers. Every one unlit.
An old Aurenne galleon, two hundred years down. The figurehead is a woman holding a lantern. Someone, long ago, gave her a face like a mother's.
A smuggler's sloop. In the hold, crates stamped PROPERTY OF C. ASHE — DO NOT OPEN. Corvin pretends not to see them.
A cot, made with hospital corners. A child's drawing is tucked under the pillow: a big woman in a hood, and the words MOTHER OSK MAKES IT STOP HURTING.
A cot, made with hospital corners. On the blanket, a single dried flower, placed very carefully.
Vigil stone
A cairn of gray stones. On the largest, chiseled by someone who was not a mason: SIR ALDOUS VENN. HE STOOD BETWEEN.
A stone knight, sword point-down, head bowed. The plinth reads: DAME ORSOLA OF THE WESTMARCH. SHE WAS AFRAID OF HORSES.
A stone knight with a cracked shield. The plinth reads: SIR TEODOR BRAND. HE WEPT AT EVERY KNIGHTING, INCLUDING HIS OWN.
A stone knight, very young, very serious. The plinth reads: SIR ALDOUS VENN, AGE NINETEEN. Somebody has scratched underneath, much later: STILL AN IDIOT. — G.T.
The Rook Queen's nest: a ring of buttons, spoons, bottle caps, a brass doorknob, three wedding rings and, right in the middle, a child-sized empty space shaped like a knife.
A kite with a lopsided sun painted on it, tangled in the junk. A name on the spar in crayon: TILLY. PROPERTY OF. KEEP OFF.
Hal's cabin
The Kingfisher's mainmast, snapped. Her colors still fly from the stump: Dawnguard blue, with a kingfisher stitched over the sunburst by someone who could not sew.
A bow gun, still loaded. The gunner's gloves are on the breech, laid down neatly side by side, as if he meant to come back for them.
A small bed with a patchwork quilt. Every patch is a different shade of yellow.
A shelf of wooden animals: a gull, a cat, a lopsided horse. Carved by a twelve-year-old, badly, with enormous care.
rift_echo${i}
A star chart, inked on sailcloth. Half the stars are crossed out. Beside the gaps, in tiny writing: "fell?" "fell." "FELL. Bother."
A copy of The Sunward Atlas, annotated in red ink by its own author. The margins are fuller than the pages.
A shelf of books about the sun. Every one ends with the same chapter title: "And Then It Rose Again."

src/data/maps/ch12_epilogue.js.s: The door is painted shut. Everything here is.
Two plates. Two cups. A third chair, pushed in, that nobody has sat in for seven years.
Your father's books. Sea charts. Star charts. A novel about a pirate queen with the last chapter torn out.

src/data/maps/ch12_evernoon.js.s: A statue of the Hierophant as a young man, arms open. The plinth reads: HE WHO KEPT THE LIGHT. Someone has scratched underneath: AND KEPT IT. AND KEPT IT.
A statue of a girl of ten holding a book against her chest. The plinth has no name on it. It doesn't need one.
Seven sockets are set into the paving before the arch, each shaped like a jagged piece of something round.
A belfry bell, toppled and cracked. Its clapper has been removed and laid neatly beside it, like a sleeping child.
A Vesper soldier's helmet, half-buried in ash. Inside, a folded note: "Mira — if the sun really stops, I'll be home for supper forever. Save me a seat." The ink has faded to violet.
A small stone at the foot of the arch. Two names, carved by an unpracticed hand: LYSA LORNE. CASSIAN LORNE. Underneath, smaller: "Now they both know where the sun goes."
Beyond the arch there is only a bright, ordinary morning, and a long way down.
Halcyon's staying tied off till this is done, sparrow. No coming back — you said it yourself.
Where Evernoon stood there is only the shard, and the wall, and a quiet morning under the new sun. The golden afternoon is gone. Nobody misses it as much as they thought they would.
dancer${n}
dancer${n}_aside
The dancer smiles at you. Somewhere, faintly, a clock is ticking.
Lemonade! Fresh lemonade! And... swords, apparently. I don't remember stocking swords. I don't remember stocking anything.
Funny. Same lemon. I've been squeezing the same lemon all afternoon.
Lovely afternoon. Lovely.
I keep meaning to go home for supper. Mira will have the soup on.
Lovely afternoon.
Two sweethearts lean toward each other. They have been leaning toward each other for forty years.
Just KISS already.
Let them have it, kid. Some moments are worth taking slow.
Forty years is not slow, Corvin. Forty years is a medical condition.
Three balls in the air above the juggler's hands. They never come down. They never go up, either.
That's the worst thing I've ever seen.
Laaaaaaaaaaaaaa—
He is holding the first note of the Dawnsong. He has been holding it for forty years. He has not taken a breath.
Did you hear? The Keeper's little girl has been asking about the purple lights by the old wall. Such a curious child.
Somebody ought to keep an eye on her tonight.
Have you seen Miss Lysa? Her brother's looking all over.
Miss Lysa! There you are, love. Your brother's been looking all over for you.
I am not her.
Miss Lysa! There you are, love.
Apples! Apples that never brown!
I'd eat one, only then there'd be one fewer. And I don't know how to grow more.
Sel's been about to win since lunch. Never shows his hand.
Somebody ought to call him. Not me. I'm comfortable.
Squire Venn! Eyes front! You'll have the Lantern plaza tonight, lad, and the Keeper won't want a squire who fidgets.
Tonight. Ha. As if tonight's ever coming.
Can't ring her. Rope's stuck fast.
You don't ring at noon, see. You ring at the turning of the hour. And the hour never turns.
You're it! ...You're it! ...You're it!
I'm not it. I've never been it. I'm never going to be it.
The bell tower. Its great bell hangs at the top of the swing, about to fall back and ring the hour. It has been about to for forty years.
An anvil with a half-forged sword on it, still glowing. The smith's hammer hangs in the air just above it.
;_our
Lysa! LYSA!
She's not by the old wall. The lights are all over the plaza now. Please — please hurry.
It's so pretty...
Get indoors! The Lantern's guttering — the dark's coming up through the drains!
Hush, hush. Keep your eyes shut, sweetheart. If you don't look at it, it can't see you.
Forty years I've walked this street, and I've never once seen the Lantern flicker.
It's flickering.
A chalk drawing on the flagstones: the sun, with a little door drawn in its side. Underneath, in a child's capitals: WHERE DOES IT GO?
A child's white shoe, the buckle undone. It is facing the wall, as if whoever wore it walked straight on without it.
Here the old city wall is thinnest. The stones don't meet. Through the cracks, violet light, and a sound like the sea a long way down.
Lysa's ribbon, on the cobbles. When Sable reaches for it, it isn't there. It was never really there.
Not yet. Everyone's by the fire. One last night first.
Not like this. We should catch our breath first.

← PORT GALE · WHISPERWOLD →
The Gale Coast Road. Mind the cliffs. Mind the wind. Mind the cliffs in the wind.

src/data/maps/ch2_port_gale.js.s: ...Is that his seal? On your letter? Oh, my. Oh, my. Then you are in good hands, child. The very best.
...A woman in Thistledown who teaches you to _change_ your Crest? Don't tease me. That's cruel.
♪ _Go not to the Whisperwold, my love, where the old trees keep the dead..._ ♪

src/data/maps/ch2_thistledown.js.s:
THISTLEDOWN — Est. by people who were tired of walking.
Inn · Trading Post · The Sage (up the hill, knock loudly, duck).
Old Bethan's up the hill, past Tobble's beehives. Knock loudly. Then duck.
...You've been up to see the heretic, haven't you? I can tell. You have that look. That _awake_ look.

src/data/maps/ch2_whisperwold.js.s: A standing stone, carved with spirals worn almost smooth. Moss has grown into the shape of a hand.

src/data/maps/ch3_aurenne.js.s:
THE RINGING BELL — Rooms · Suppers · Songs.
No rooks.

THE LANTERN QUARTER.
Residents only after dusk. (We mean it.)

LOW TOWN.
Mind the mud. Mind your purse. Mind your business.

src/data/maps/ch3_interiors.js.s: The little ones are scrubbing my pots. Never seen pots so clean, or children so proud of it. Bed and supper, Page? Forty gold.
Welcome to the Ringing Bell! Bed, supper, and a bard who knows four songs. Forty gold.
the Ringing Bell
A song for the island folk? I know four. Three are about drinking. Here's the other one.
♪ _The festival lanterns were hung in a row, / and the Keeper's two children ran laughing below._ ♪
♪ _Then the great light went out like a breath on a flame, / and the dark came to Aurenne and called them by name._ ♪
♪ _He held up the Lantern, the Keeper so true — / and the city was saved, and a girl was lost too._ ♪
Not my best rhyme. The Choir doesn't care for it, so naturally it's the one everybody asks for.
Off duty. Which means I'm not here, and you didn't see me.
If the Lord-Commander asks, I'm on patrol. This tankard is the patrol.
Wait. Kestrel? Venn's squire? Dawn, man, everyone said you went soft on some island.
I went _salty._ It's different.
The Ringing Bell has the best stew in the city. It's also the only stew in the city that's never made anyone ill.
These are related facts.
Marta says I can have pie if I scrub ALL the pots. I've scrubbed all the pots twice.
Is it pie time? It feels like pie time.
I don't remember being down there. Nell says that's good.
I can do bows now. On my shoes. Pip showed me. Double-knots are for babies.
Marta says we can stay. Dishes for beds. She doesn't sing, I checked.
Look after him, Fish-Bird. He thinks he's a prince. He's mostly just loud.
A brass bell over the bar. A card beneath it: RING FOR SERVICE. DON'T RING FOR FUN. WE MEAN YOU, TERRENCE.
A pot of stew big enough to bathe in. It smells of rosemary and something brown and comforting.
The Hierophant's Page! Going south? You'll want boots, water, and something sharp. I sell two of those.
Bellwright Arms & Sundries. Swords, salves, and the finest bell-bronze buckles in Aurenne.
A bell-founder's anvil, cracked clean through. Oswin keeps it "for sentiment." There is a price tag on it anyway.
Ledgers going back three generations of Bellwrights. The earliest entry: ONE (1) BELL, LARGE. PAID IN GEESE.
His Holiness is waiting for you in his study, Page. The left-hand door.
The Hierophant's study is through the left-hand door at the back. The archives, the right.
Brother Quill keeps the archives. He is older than some of the books and fonder of them than of people.
Welcome, pilgrim. The dawn-office is long over, but the light is always open.
I pray for my son every day. He's a sailor.
The Choir says the sea belongs to the Gloam after dark. So I pray very loudly at dusk.
Shh. I'm listening for the Dawnsong. You can hear it in here, if you're quiet.
...You're not being quiet.
Sister Mercy's name has been struck from the rolls. I struck it myself. My hand would not stop shaking.
Forty-one admitted. None discharged. How did none of us ever do the arithmetic?
One Crest, one life, one light. It is carved under St. Aurel's feet. We say it every dawn.
I have said it eleven thousand times. I counted. That is my Crest, I think: Counter.
St. Aurel, holding up the first Lantern. Carved beneath her feet: *ONE CREST · ONE LIFE · ONE LIGHT.*
A pillar carved with the Seven Lanterns, from Lanternfall in the west to Skyreach above the storm. Someone has rubbed Lanternfall's carving smooth with their thumb, over many years.
The Hierophant's study. The acolyte by the altar would know if you're expected.
A painting hangs on the wall beneath a white sheet. Not a speck of dust on it. Someone uncovers it often.
...It's not ours to lift.
Letters, stacked neatly on the desk. The one on top is in your own handwriting: your letter about the stars, from two winters ago.
He kept it.
An armillary sphere of brass rings. Where the little golden sun should sit at its center, there is only an empty socket.
Treatises on the Dawnsong, scored and annotated in a fine hand. One spine has been read until it broke: *On the Inversion of Hymns.*
Correspondence with the Keepers, filed by Lantern. The Lanternfall folder is very thin. On top, in Ysolde's hand, one word: NO.
...No, I don't know where the bestiaries are. I've been looking for the bestiaries since spring.
Misfiled between a hymnal and a cookbook: a loose page.

"...and so the Seven Lanterns were raised along the edge of the world, that the Hearthsun might never lose its way home. Each Keeper sings her own light. The Grand Lantern of Aurenne, first and eldest, sings for the city, and for the six."
A shelf of hymnals. And one cookbook, which explains the stains.
In a locked box marked LONG NIGHT — DO NOT LEND: a single page.
"At the turning of the summer festival, the Grand Lantern failed. The Gloam came into Aurenne through the dark, as water fills a footprint. Three hundred and twelve were taken before dawn."
Restricted shelves: Lantern schematics, Keepers' confessions, and one very old, very angry letter from Lanternfall.
*A Lexicon of Crests*, with margin notes in four different hands, arguing about Gloamweaver. None of them agree on anything, except that it should not exist.
I exist.
A tuning anvil. Forty years of bells were tuned on it. There is a dent in it shaped like a word you can't quite read.
A ledger of every noon since Tolliver began. Every entry reads RANG TRUE — except seven that read FLAT — and then, today, in large shaky letters: RANG TRUE!!!
A ledger of every noon since Tolliver began. Every entry reads RANG TRUE. Except the last seven, which read FLAT. FLAT. FLAT. FLAT. FLAT. FLAT. FLAT.
A suit of Dawnguard plate on a stand, polished to a mirror. There is a notch in the breastplate, over the heart, that has never been hammered out.
A portrait: a broad, laughing knight with a ridiculous mustache, and a young woman trying very hard not to laugh with him.
Mm. Warm. So warm.
They said I'd never be cold again.
Sister Mercy says if I'm good, I can go downstairs where it's warm.
I'm being SO good.
The Sisters stay under watch until the Lord-Commander says otherwise.
They keep offering me soup. I keep saying no. It's the longest conversation I've ever had.
The almshouse ledger, in a neat round hand. ADMITTED: forty-one. DISCHARGED: none. Beside each name, a small mark like a closed eye.
Leek and barley soup. It smells wonderful. Under the wonderful, faintly, something sweet and sleepy.
Poppy-milk. Enough to make a grown man very, very agreeable. Nobody eat the soup.

src/data/maps/ch3_rooftops.js.s: Charcoal drawings on the bell tower wall: four stick-children wearing crowns. Under them, in careful letters: *THE GUTTER CORT · PIP · NELL · TUCK · WICK.* Two of the crowns have been rubbed out and drawn back in, darker.
...Don't look at that. That's private property. Of the Court.
From up here you can see the whole City of Bells: the Cathedral, the Grand Lantern, and far off to the south, the brown thread of the Pilgrim Road.
The bells will ring at noon! And at noon tomorrow! And the noon after that!
What a summer, eh? Feels like it'll never end.
Lysa! Your brother's looking for you. He's _always_ looking for you.
Hush — the Keeper's going up. Watch the gallery. It's the best part.

src/data/maps/ch3_undercroft.js.s: blocker:c3_uc_sewers:c3_crack
The brickwork here bulges outward, cracked and sweating. There is a hollow sound behind it.
Bram. Would you?
With _pleasure._
I have been wanting to hit something that didn't hit back for _days._
Scratched into the brick in chalk, at about the height of an eleven-year-old: PIP WAS ERE.
...That's from last year. I was _exploring._
A child's shoe, much too small for anyone who should be down here. The laces are still tied — in a double knot.
That's Wick's. He does double knots because he can't do bows. I keep telling him. I keep _telling_ him.
A gray hooded lantern, dropped and cracked. The Sisters of Small Mercies carry ones just like it.
A sheet of music, soaked through. The notes run from right to left.
Sable reads it, and hums. The hum makes your back teeth ache.
It is the Dawnsong. Backwards.
The names are worn almost smooth. Under every one, the same date: THE LONG NIGHT.
A family tomb: a mother, a father, and four small names in a row. Someone has left a wooden toy horse on it. It is very old.
Tucked under a guttered candle on the last tomb: a loose, water-stained page.
"...the Keeper, Aldric Lorne, was in the lamp-room when the light failed. He might have gone down to the square, where his daughter {dim|████} was. He chose the Lantern. The city lived."
The great bell of the old foundry, cracked from crown to lip. Whatever was ringing it wanted very badly to be heard.
A woman curled on a cot, humming. When you say hello, she says it back — in exactly your voice.
An old man counting on his fingers. He gets to nine and starts again. He has been doing it, he says, for a very long time. Or possibly since this morning.
This cell is empty, except for a pair of boots standing neatly side by side. The boots are still warm.
Mercy's notes, in a neat round hand:
_Subject 31: no resistance. Children rarely resist — their memories are short and sweet. The body accepts the Gloam if it is given a memory to hold. Without one, the Gloam makes only beasts._
_Day 40. Another beast. What did HE do differently? What did he give her to hold?_
"He." Who's "he"?
Her boss, maybe. Everyone's got a boss.
Sable says nothing at all.
A cot with leather straps. The straps are child-sized.
Pressed inside one of Mercy's ledgers, a page from an old chronicle, annotated in red ink.
In the margin, in fresh red ink: _Not lost. Only waiting._
The crucible. At the bottom, a residue like burnt sugar, and a smell like a summer afternoon.

src/data/maps/ch4a_desert.js.s:
THE PILGRIM ROAD — east to Saltglass.
Carry water. Carry more water than that.
Walking to Saltglass to hear the blind Keeper. They say she can name your Crest before the Lantern does.
They say she told the Hierophant something once that made him leave in the middle of the night.
I'd like to know what. I'd like to know anything, really. That's why I walk.
Ysmay's water is the last sweet water for thirty leagues. After that it's the oasis, or the town, or you drink sand.
Mind the glass flats. Folk see things out there. Then they walk toward them.
A Choir milestone: AURENNE — 40 LEAGUES. SALTGLASS — 30.
Below, older letters someone tried to chisel away: "...WHERE THE LIGHT GOES, WE GO."
Pilgrim's Arch
Pilgrim's Arch
A pilgrims' cairn. Every stone has a name scratched on it. Some of the names are very small, like children wrote them.
Sarn says we're not thieves. We're a toll road with knives.
The ribs of a giant wyrm arch out of the sand like the frame of a ship nobody finished building.
A weathered statue of a Keeper, holding a lamp above her head. The wind has worn away her face.
There is a cup of water at her feet. It is still cool.
Saltglass is east... but that smoke in the north. Someone could be hurt out there.
Lift-glass housing
The mainmast. Someone has carved a tally into it — dozens of little marks — and, at the top, a single word: STAY.
The foremast, splintered halfway up. A torn sail flaps from it like a flag of surrender. Or a very tired wave.
Cargo crates stamped with a dozen different port seals. Half of them are empty. The other half are labeled "DEFINITELY NOT CONTRABAND."

src/data/maps/ch4a_greyspine.js.s:
GREYSPINE PASS — Frosthollow, a day's climb.
WALK SOFTLY. THE SNOW LISTENS.

QUIET WAY. Do not run. Do not shout.
Do not sing, Brother Tolle.
QUIET WAY. The snow above has been waiting all winter. Do not give it a reason.
Resting my knees. They're older than the rest of me.
Gray cloaks passed me on the lower trail two days ago. Forty of them, with a big man in front who never looked at the view.
Who climbs a mountain and doesn't look at the view?
Vigil Stone
Frozen pack
A shrine to the Keepers of Frosthollow. Pilgrims have tied strips of cloth to it — prayers, names, a child's mitten.
Frost lily
c4a_lily_${i}

FROSTHOLLOW. Pilgrims welcome. Beds free.
The goats are not for petting. (They bite.)
Came up for the Keeper's blessing. Stayed for the soup.
There's an army camped at the foot of the mountain. Sunburst banners. Holy soldiers, I thought — but I watched them a whole evening, and they never once prayed.
Sweep, sweep. I keep sweeping the steps to the tower.
Nobody climbs them now. I sweep them anyway. Somebody should keep the way clear.
Snow, snow, snow. Sweep, sweep, sweep.
The mountain is very generous with its snow. I am very generous with my broom. We have an understanding.
Run, Halloway. It's what Keepers' children are good at.
The Bell Stair, Wren! GO!
vesper_g${i}
Bell tower
The well is frozen over. Someone has chipped a hole in the ice and left a ladle beside it, the way you'd leave a key under a mat.
Gate road's crawling with gray cloaks, sparrow. Wrong way.
The Ice Score
I keep airing the beds. Tolle would want them aired.
He wrote from Saltglass. Two pages about the children and one line about himself: "I am managing." He underlined "managing." That boy.
A guest book. Three winters back, in a big looping hand: "Sir Aldous Venn and squire. Couldn't sleep. Lovely tea."
Steps cut into the ice by hand, worn down in the middle by centuries of monks' feet. Each step has a number carved beside it. You are on step four hundred and twelve.
A little bell is carved into the wall by the Hearthstone, and under it: FOR THE ONES WHO HAD TO LEAVE IN A HURRY.
blocker:c4a_frost_caves:rubble
Boots on the stair behind us. There's no going back.

src/data/maps/ch4a_saltglass.js.s:
SALTGLASS — last sweet water for thirty leagues.
The Lantern is open to pilgrims from dawn until dusk.
Caravans north: ask at the yard.
Caravan Market! Everything that came across the sand and survived it.
Prices are fixed. Fixed by me. Daily. Sometimes hourly.
Teo hasn't stopped sulking since your little friend came out of the Lantern glowing.
Thirty days until his birthday. I'm going to need a bigger sulk-bucket.
We walked from Thistledown so my Teo could be Kindled in Saltglass light. His grandfather was. And his grandfather.
Now we wait thirty days for his birthday, in a town where water costs more than wine.
We're playing Lanterns and Gloam! I'm the Gloam! RAAAH!
Rafi is ALWAYS the Gloam. He says the Gloam is the best part.
The Gloam is NOT the best part. The best part is when the sun comes back.
The children sing on the Lantern steps every morning. The Keeper sits with them.
She says it's the worst choir she's ever heard. She cried the first time.
Yrsa looks up at you and hums three notes of the morning hymn. Then she goes back to drawing a bell in the sand.
The deep well of Saltglass. The rope goes down, and down, and down.
You drop a pebble. Four heartbeats later, very faintly: _plink._
Master Ruel's furnace. The air above it wobbles like a mirage that can't make up its mind.
The Lamp
The lamp of Saltglass burns inside a cage of saltglass panes. The light comes out of the glass in every direction at once.
Up close it hums — low, like a cat that's pleased with itself. Or a cat that isn't.
A mirror of polished saltglass. Your reflection is a half-step behind you, as if it's thinking things over.
A mirror of polished saltglass. In it, the Lantern's light looks like dawn. In the room, it looks like noon.
A cool bed, a cold supper, and a jug of real water? Sixty gold. The water alone is worth forty.
the Cool Well
The Hierophant's men used to ride through and bless the wells.
Now they ride through and _count_ them. Why would you count wells? Wells don't go anywhere.
...Unless you expect to need every one of them.
I'm writing a ballad about the Sunscar. So far it rhymes "sand" with "sand" eleven times.
Critics call it "accurate."
I used to run the salt road in four days. Now I walk to the well and back and call it a day's work.
Best days of my life, then and now. Only now's got Nim in it.
Papa came home! He was SO dirty. Mama made him take two baths.
I drew you a picture. It's you, and the big one, and the girl with black hair, and the little one with the Crest. The little one is the biggest because he asked.
A shelf of maps — salt roads, caravan wells, wind patterns — all annotated in a quick, slanted hand. "J." in every corner.
blocker:c4a_glass_caverns:queen_door
blocker:c4a_glass_caverns:jorah_wall
Can you— is there a way through? Please. Please, I have a daughter.
Singing pillar
Singing pillar
Singing pillar
Humming wall
Humming wall
Humming wall
Glass door
A spring bubbles up through a crack in the glass. The water tastes of salt and, faintly, of thunder.
An egg of saltglass as big as a barrel. Something inside is curled up, waiting for a warmer century.
Copper pots, a wagon wheel, a child's wooden horse. A whole caravan's worth of things, polished smooth by sand.

src/data/maps/ch4b_mirefen.js.s: mp,

GREYSPINE PASS — WEST.
Someone has scratched underneath, fresh: _CLOSED. SNOW._
A girl with a black bob came out here with a bucket of something foul and made us all drink it.
I can breathe. I'd kiss her, but she looked like she'd stab me.
We were walking to Mirefen for Mother Osk's blessing. Got as far as the fever.
They won't let us in the village. Can't say I blame them. Look at my hands.
_(The veins on his wrists are black, like ink in water.)_
Da's veins are going pink again. Pink! I never thought I'd be glad of pink.
The Choir men came by on a white barge, three weeks back. Da waved to them for help.
They didn't stop. They had something in a box that hummed.
A statue of a woman with a lantern, up to her knees in the fen. A string of dried frogs hangs around her neck. An offering, or a joke. In Mirefen it is hard to tell.
Gaspar's punt. The pole is worn smooth as bone where his hands go.
That's the way back to the mountains.
...There's nothing back there now. Come on.

MIREFEN. Mind the gaps. Mind the water. Mind your manners.
By order of Mother Osk, Keeper of the Mirefen Light.
Business is back! Well. People are buying soap again. That's how you know a town's recovering — soap.
Buying? Selling? Coughing? Two out of three, I can help.
Benet caught an eel this morning with two heads. Both of them looked healthy, though. That's progress.
The Choir barge came the night Mother Osk took the fever. Very polite. Very white robes.
Left the next morning. The Lantern's been dark since. Funny, that.
Benet says I shouldn't say "funny." Benet says a lot of things.
Corla's telling everyone about the two-headed eel, isn't she.
It had one head. The other one was a stick. I didn't have the heart.
Don't listen to Corla. The Choir are holy folk.
Mind you, holy folk don't usually take the light with them when they leave.
Osk's sitting up and complaining about the soup. She'll outlive us all out of spite.
Here — I'm weaving her a new blanket. The old one's been in the bog. Don't ask.
Sixty years I've known Osk. She's been dying three times and refused every time.
This time she's too tired to argue. That's what frightens me.
I'm playing Keepers and Gloam! I'm the Gloam. Rarrr.
Nettie's the Keeper. She's better now. She keeps winning.
The Drownmere's due south, straight past me. Take the punt. Bring it back — it's the only one that doesn't leak.
And if you see my brother in the water... don't talk to him. He's been dead nine years.
Nobody goes into the Drownmere. Not since the light went out. Doctor's orders.
A sack of willow bark, half-boiled. Doctor Vey's handwriting on the label: _does nothing. try anyway._
A cauldron of something gray. It smells like hope, if hope had been left out overnight.
Mag Tiller's stall: eel-skin boots, reed charms, a jar labeled ROT CURE (GENUINE). The jar is empty. The label is very confident.
A rain barrel, carefully covered. Everyone in Mirefen drinks rainwater now. Nobody trusts the fen.
Nobody goes into the Drownmere. Turn around, please.
We're not leaving. Not while she's like this.
They say the Marrow girl walked into the Drownmere and walked out carrying its heart in a jar.
I'm switching to tea.
Black veins. That's how it starts. Then the cough. Then you start seeing people in the fog.
I've got the cough. Haven't seen anyone yet.
Except you lot. Are you real?
A pot of eel stew. Rusk swears there's nothing in it but eel. Rusk is not looking at you when he says it.
A shelf of books swollen fat with damp. _The Keepers of Old_, _Fen Remedies_, and a romance called _The Heron's Kiss_ with one page dog-eared to death.
The cradle
The brass cradle where Mirefen's Dawnstone should sleep. Empty. Osk has put a jar of fireflies in it, out of spite.
The brass cradle at the heart of the Lantern. Empty. The metal is still warm in the shape of something that is not there.
Jars of herbs, eel-oil, dried frogs and something labeled in Osk's cramped hand: _DO NOT. EVER. (YES, YOU, HESK.)_
A cauldron, scrubbed clean. Somebody has been making soup every day for a woman who cannot eat it.
blocker:c4b_drownmere:rotwall
A statue of a Keeper, half swallowed by the bog. Her lantern is full of frogspawn. The frogs, at least, seem happy.
The Sunken Shrine. Someone kept a lamp burning here for two hundred years, until the fen rose. You can still see the soot on the stones.

src/data/maps/ch4b_stormcrown.js.s: s flight, Skyreach, Vasha
A mooring post as thick as a man, scorched black on the side that faces the mountain. Lightning loves this place.
The Halcyon's mainmast. A tally of little lightning bolts is carved into it. Forty-one. The last one is very fresh, and very deep.
The Gull's Nest — highest beds in Solmere! Eighty gold. The view's free. The vertigo's also free.
the Gull's Nest
Windward Exchange! Everything up here came up on a ship, so everything up here costs a ship's worth. Have a browse.
The isle's risen a full fathom since this morning. I could feel it in my knees.
Skyreach floats on light, they say. Seems it can float on stubbornness too, in a pinch.
Skyreach floats on the Lantern's light, child. Has done for three hundred years.
And the light holds the Thunderhead down beneath us. Two jobs, one Lantern. That's the old story.
The Ardent says it's just a story. The Ardent gave our stone away. I'm old. I notice things.
You went down beneath the isle for us. Even though you think the Hierophant is wrong.
I don't know what to do with that. I have been praying about it. The wind has not answered.
When the Vespersong is sung, no one will ever be lost to the storm again. No more empty chairs at supper.
Don't you want that? Doesn't everyone want that?
Ilka's put Skyreach-cut lift-crystals in that old tub. She'll climb like a lark now.
Your captain flew her up through the Stormcrown on _desert glass_. Nobody up here will ever buy him a drink again — they'll be too busy telling the story.
I saw you come up through the storm. Thought you were a falling barn.
Then I thought: no, a barn would fly better.
The Lord-Commander came on a black warship, three weeks back. The Ardent handed him our stone on the steps of the Lantern, and everybody cheered.
I cheered. Loudest of anyone.
...I don't know why I cheered.
A fountain fed by rain-catchers. Coins glint at the bottom: offerings to the wind, for safe flights. There are a great many coins.
The Halcyon, nose-down in what used to be Ilka's shed. One mast is broken. The other is somehow holding a chicken.
Ilka's yard. Where the Halcyon crashed, there is a neat pile of salvaged timber labeled, in large letters, CORVIN'S. YOU'RE PAYING FOR THIS.
The Keel Lift's for the Keel-crew only. Ardent's orders.
The cradle
In the brass cradle where Skyreach's Dawnstone should sit, a single silver tuning fork stands upright, humming to itself.
You know that note. You have been carrying it in your pack for weeks.

blocker:c4b_undercradle:gate2
blocker:c4b_undercradle:gate3

src/data/maps/ch4b_verdance.js.s:
THE THORNWOOD.
Keeper's grove beyond. Walk softly; the trees are listening.
_(Underneath, newer, in charcoal: CLOSED. THORNS. DO NOT.)_
Forage, fletching, and things that fix you. Mostly the first two. Have a look.
The Hollow Log. Hollow log, soft moss, warm stew. Seventy gold, and I'll even let you choose which log.
the Hollow Log
The soldiers came a month back. Fifty of them, white and gold, the Hierophant's sun on every shield.
The big one with the beard didn't even go in. Sat on my woodpile eating our apples while his men carried the Keeper's light out in a box.
Didn't pay for the apples, either.
You've seen her? Truly? Is she— is she very old?
Of course she is. I only meant — is she very _kind_? I always imagined she was.
I'm writing an epic about Keeper Elowen. Nobody in Rootholm has seen her in thirty years.
Some say she is four hundred years old. Some say she has turned into a tree. I have rhymed both possibilities, just in case.
I'm not allowed in the Tangle anymore. Or near the Tangle. Or near anyone who's been near the Tangle.
Mum's very thorough.
I tied a ribbon for Gran on the Memory Tree. A yellow one. She liked yellow.
The pretty lights in the forest weren't her. Ilse said. Ilse says it's all right to miss her anyway.
When I'm sixteen I'm going to be a Warden like the big one. Or a Rogue like the small one.
He said I could be both. He said that's allowed now. Is that allowed now?
The Memory Tree
The Memory Tree
Fern's crates: bundles of arrows fletched with jay feathers, jars of honey, a sign reading NO HAGGLING, and under it, smaller: (a little haggling).
blocker:c4b_thornwood:thornA
blocker:c4b_thornwood:thornB
blocker:c4b_thornwood:thornC
A statue of a Keeper, so old that her face has worn smooth. Somebody — recently — has put a crown of daisies on her head.
The Lantern
The Lantern of Thornwood. Roots have climbed it to the gallery; blossom grows inside the lamp-glass.
The cradle at its heart is empty. A bird has started a nest in it.
The trees here grow too close to pass. For now.

src/data/maps/ch5_dungeons.js.s: A worn grave-slab: BRENNA HALLOWAY — FIRST OF US — SHE CUT THE STAIR.
ODA HALLOWAY. SHE HELD THE LIGHT THROUGH THE STORM OF THE SEVENTY BOATS, AND ALL SEVENTY CAME HOME.
IDE HALLOWAY. "SHE SANG FLAT AND NEVER ONCE MISSED A DAWN." Your grandmother. You remember her hands, and her terrible singing.
A blank slab, smoothed and ready. Nothing carved on it yet.
A small, newer stone, the letters cut in a careful, narrow hand you know very well: EDRIN — WHO WAS NOT A KEEPER, BUT KEPT US.
The first Keeper, worn faceless by four hundred years of damp. Fresh candle stubs at her feet. Someone comes down here often. Someone who comes down from the top.
The great lamp of Lanternfall. Its bed of brass is empty.

src/data/maps/ch5_lanternfall.js.s: No time. RUN.
The Lantern door is barred from inside. White light leaks from every crack.

LANTERNFALL — Westmost Light of Solmere.
Chalked beneath, in a soldier's square capitals: HARMONIZATION IN PROGRESS. KEEP TO YOUR HOMES.
_(He doesn't look at you. He's looking at the sun.)_
Move along, miss. Please.
That hum. Does it ever stop? It's in my teeth.
I've swept my step eleven times today, Wren.
Every time I look up, the sun's still there. Watching me sweep.
Wren! Remember me? Kindling day, right before you — Ranger! I've been practicing every morning.
Everyone's acting like the world's ending. It's just a really long sunset. ...Right?
One Crest, one life, girl. And one sun, one sky.
Something up there has forgotten the rules. Eighty years, and I've never seen the sky forget the rules.
My Tamsy's been up all night with folk who say the hum gives them headaches.
She says it isn't a headache. She says it's like remembering something you never did.
Tide went out at noon yesterday. Hasn't come back.
You can walk to the eel rocks now. You can walk to the rocks past the eel rocks. Sea's holding its breath, girl. Long breath.
The Hierophant asked us to wait with the ship. He said tonight we would see the most beautiful sunset of our lives.
He said, "Remember it."
...Why would he tell us to remember it?
Tobias won't come in for supper. Says the boat needs readying. He's readied it four times.
Talk to him, Wren. He listens to Halloways. Always did.
The village well. WREN + ILSE + THE SEA, carved years ago. Underneath, freshly scratched, the knife marks still pale: + PIP.
Wrong way, sparrow! The DOCKS!
The tide caves... Tobias would know if there's another way up. Ask him first.
The tide caves. Not now. Mom first.
No time! Down the hill!
Your own shelf. Every book on it washed up on the beach. You used to think the sea liked you.
Your bed. Made. Mom made your bed. She never makes your bed.
Bread box
Ilse's herb jars, labeled in her tiny, exact handwriting. Nana has kept every one of them dusted while she was away.
The kettle. Nana Brisa has had it on the boil since yesterday noon, just in case.
Wren, love! A bed and a bowl of chowder? Thirty gold. Prices went up — the sun's making everyone nervous.
the Gull's Rest
Forty years at sea, and I was never once frightened of calm water.
Till today.
Wren! Homecoming special: everything's the same price as always.
A crate of salted fish and a note: "MAELA — DON'T." Below it: "I DID." Below that, newer: "TOBY — THE BOAT'S FINE. COME IN FOR SUPPER."
A charcoal sketch pinned over the stove: three skinny boys in a rowboat, grinning. Under each, a name: EDRIN. TOBY. FEN.

src/data/maps/ch6_shards.js.s: The cot you have slept in for a year. Someone has patched the blanket a dozen times, with whatever was to hand. One patch is a piece of a Dawnguard flag.
A pot of soup, gently burning. It smells of ash-potato and, very faintly, of fish.
A cairn of stacked gray stones. Scratched on the flat stone at its foot: EDRIN HALLOWAY. HE'D WANT A BETTER STONE.
A newer cairn. The stones are still sharp-edged. YSOLDE HALLOWAY. KEEPER. SHE HELD.
A little fishing boat, upright on the ash, a long way from any water. Painted on the bow: THE SEAGULL. Fennick's boat. It rose with the sea, and came down here, with him.
Fennick's garden. Ash-potatoes, a stubborn rosemary, and — tucked in a sheltered corner — one sprig of sea lavender, in a pot, carefully watered.
A practice post, hacked half through. Fennick's been keeping his arm in. Or keeping busy.
Not yet. Fennick wanted to show me something first.

LANTERNFALL — Westmost Light of Solmere.
The chalk underneath has almost weathered away: ...ONIZATION IN PROGRE... KEEP TO YOUR HOMES.
The village well, torn up roots and all. WREN + ILSE + THE SEA + PIP. Somebody has added, in the last year, very small: COME HOME.
Look west
Your bed, still made. Your mother made it the morning she wrote the letter. Nobody has slept in it since.
The cutter's mast, snapped clean. A Dawnguard pennant still flutters from the stump, red and gold, very bright against the ash.

A sheet of white Choir paper, the gold sunburst at its head:
THE LAST STONE WAS GIVEN FREELY, BY THE KEEPER'S DAUGHTER OF LANTERNFALL.
— by order of His Radiance the Hierophant.
Someone has drawn a noose underneath.
Don't steal, don't fight, don't fall off. That's the whole law.
Folk keep falling off. You'd think it'd be the easy one.
Warden says you're going east. Alone.
I'll keep the soup warm. Hale says I'm not to say that. I said it anyway.
East gate's shut. Strait's shut. Everything east of here's shut.
Warden Hale's orders. Ask at the big hull, north side.
Salvage and sundries! Everything I sell fell out of the sky, so it's all slightly dented.
Some of it's even better than new. The sky's full of dead rich men's luggage.
Seven wounds in the sky, child. I count them every hour. Somebody has to.
Six of them bleed white. One bleeds gold — far to the west, low down, near where Lanternfall was.
Somebody over there is still holding on to something. Holding very, very hard.
Twenty years a sailor out of Port Gale. Now look up. No — UP. See that shimmer, past the wounds?
That's the sea. All of it. Hanging up there, upside down, fish and all.
Now and then a fish falls out. Free dinner, if it doesn't land on you.
Ash-potatoes. They grow in anything. Taste of nothing. Keep you alive.
Like most things now, I suppose.
We're playing Lost Wall! Kay writes letters and I deliver them. It's way better than the other game.
We're playing Catch the Keeper's Girl! You be her! You have to run, and if we catch you, we throw you off the edge!
...PRETEND off the edge. Kay always cries if it's real off the edge.
I don't like that game. I think the Keeper's girl was probably just sad.
Mama says sad people do stupid things. Mama did one once. She married Papa.
Trader, out of Kiteholm. North, past the wind-stacks. Town of kites and scrap.
A gang of orphans runs the scrap-yards there. Boss is a boy — twelve, maybe. Mouth like a sailor, fingers like a magpie. He took my purse, then gave it back because I "looked like I needed it more."
And a big blond sellsword who drinks too much and cries at sea shanties. Kiteholm's a strange place.
I come out here to the edge every morning and I count to a hundred.
I don't jump. I just count. Then I go back and eat my soup.
It's a good number, a hundred. You should try it.
Letters, pinned three deep. "MAMA — I'M ON THE BIG ROCK. THERE'S SOUP." "TO WHOEVER HAS MY DOG: HIS NAME IS BISCUIT."
"DAD — I KEPT THE BOAT. I KEPT IT. COME AND SEE." "To Corporal Hask, if you're alive: I forgive you for the thing with the goat."
Lost Wall
Right in the middle of the wall: "Dear Sun." And beside it, a small square of paper signed only "— W."
Hundreds of letters to people nobody can find. The paper rustles in the ash-wind like a flock of birds that cannot quite take off.
"Bram — if a girl with red hair asks, tell her I'm sorry I never wrote back." The handwriting is shaky. There's no name.
Maela's kettle. Big enough to bathe a pony in. Always full. Always gray.
A cot and a cup of something hot. Forty gold. The beds are hammocks. Don't ask what the hammocks used to be.
the Upturned Keel
There was a sky-captain through here, back in the spring. Tried to buy a whole barrel of rum on a promise.
Said he had a ship. Said she was grounded at some place called the Roost. Said a lot of things. Sang most of them.
We play for ash-potatoes. Stakes are high. Very high. I'm down eleven potatoes.
Funny. Nothing to buy, and we still gamble.
The bar: a ship's rail laid across two barrels. A brass bell hangs over it. Nobody rings it. Nobody likes bells anymore.

A chart of the Shattered Sea, drawn on the back of a sail. Shards marked in charcoal. Most of them have notes: HOUNDS. GLASS. DON'T. One, far to the east, just says: AURENNE? and underneath, smaller: HOSPITAL.
A man asleep under a thin blanket. A gray patch has crept up his neck like frost on a window. Gloam-rot.
Bridge is down. Gods help you.
If you see the Unmoored... don't look it in the eye. It looks back. It remembers things.
Salvager, once. North spoke's the Chainyard — winch is on the old deck. South spoke's the Psalm — winch is in the deckhouse.
Turn both and the strait bridge comes down. I'd do it myself, but I like being alive. It's a habit.
The Gilded Psalm's mainmast, snapped off at the deck. Gold leaf still clings to it. The Choir built its ships to be looked at.
A chain-lock as big as a barrel, padlocked to the bridge. The chain runs away north, toward the Chainyard.
A second chain-lock. This chain runs south, toward the wreck of the Psalm.

src/data/maps/ch7_aurenne.js.s:
ASH SQUARE NOTICES
· Water: one bucket per family. Ask Sorrel.
· Violet under the skin? The Ember Ward. NOW.
· The Undercroft is SEALED. — S.
· BOUNTY: the thing in the Reliquary. See Sorrel.
Ward supply's open, and for once it's got supplies. The Ward Mother's friends pay what it costs. That's the friend discount.
Ward supply. Everything costs more than it's worth, because everything's worth more than it costs. Don't think about it too hard.
Soup's got salt in it today. Real salt! Somebody's been generous with somebody.
Eat, girl. You've the look of someone who forgets.
Ash soup. Ash bread. Ash, if you're still hungry after.
Don't make that face. It's warm, and warm is the only flavor that matters now.
Did you HEAR it? It went BONNNG. Osric says he'll teach me to ring it when my arms are long enough.
My arms are growing. I checked this morning.
I'm playing bells. _Tonk. Tonk._ That's a tin can, but you have to pretend.
Mum says the real bells were so loud you couldn't hear yourself think. I think a lot. I'd like a break.
I was an acolyte. Third Choir, tenor. I wore white.
I sang the Vespersong that night. Not in the Lantern — just in the nave, with three hundred others. We didn't know. We thought it was a hymn for a long summer.
I burned my robes. People here know anyway. They let me carry water. I think that's worse than if they spat.
I know exactly what he means.
Dawnguard. Was. Garrick's lot went up to the Noon Spire with the Hierophant. The rest of us took off our tabards and learned to dig latrines.
Kestrel? Bram Kestrel? The squire who froze at his trial? Ha — I knew him. Big lad. Good lad, for a coward.
Heard he's swinging a sword for a scrap baron up at Kiteholm now. Heard he drinks. Can't say I blame him.
Jory wants to go to Kiteholm. "There's wind up there," he says. "Wind means weather. Weather means maybe a morning."
I told him there are no mornings anymore. He said that's what everybody said about the bells.
Ada thinks I'm a dreamer. Ada married a dreamer. Ada should've read the label.
If the Ward Mother can make medicine out of a flooded hole, I can find a morning on a kite.
My husband was on the far side of the bridge when the city broke away.
I come every evening. It's always evening. So I'm always here.
Our Ward Mother, going below? With _you_?
Then you'd better bring her back, or there's an old woman in Ash Square who will learn to swing a poker.
Come sit by the fire, girl. I tell the children stories so they don't ask questions.
Once upon a time, the sun came up every morning. They don't believe me. Neither do I, some days.
Overflow cots. When the hall fills, the Ward comes outside. When the outside fills, we stop counting.
The Ward Mother hasn't slept a whole night since she got here. I've checked. I sleep across her door.
Sunsalt. Tastes like licking a hot coin. Best thing I've had in my mouth in a year, and I was married forty.
I'm on the outside cots. That means I'm getting better. Or worse. Nobody says which.
The Lantern
The Lantern
The Lantern
The Bellwrights' Tenor tower, snapped off at the shoulder. Up in the ruined belfry, one great bell still hangs. It has no clapper. It sways in the ember-wind without a sound.
Saint Aurel the Tuner, patron of the Choir. Someone has knocked off her head and set a cooking pot in its place. It's a good pot.
Saint Lumen, holding up a lantern of stone. Underneath, scratched into the plinth: HE SAID IT WOULD BE NOON FOREVER.
Driftwood markers with names chalked on them. Some have little things left on top: a spoon, a ribbon, a single boot.
Driftwood markers with names chalked on them — and around every one, a ring of tiny gold-green shoots pushing up through the ash. Dawnmoss.
The east bridge ends in nothing. Far, far below, through the violet haze, something glitters — another shard, maybe. Maybe a whole country, falling slower than you.
A doorframe with no house behind it. Somebody has hung a wreath of wire and rag flowers on it, and swept the step.
The common soup pot. It smells of ash and onion and, faintly, of hope. Mostly ash.
When I'm better, I'm going to be a Vanguard. Like Wren.
Ilse says I can be anything. She said it like she was cross about it.
...Wren? You're real? I thought the rot was making me see things again.
Everybody from home is gone except me and Ilse. Ilse says that makes us family. She says it angry, but I think she means it.
She's doing better. The Ward Mother sat with her all last night. She sits with everyone, one night each, in turn.
I don't know when she sleeps. I don't think she knows either.
My hand's pink again. Pink! I've never been so happy to look like a boiled ham.
Cut my hand on a scrap of the old Cathedral. A _holy_ scrap. Didn't help.
Ward Mother says the violet's stopped at my wrist. She says it like a promise. She doesn't make promises.
That girl with the bun? Ilse? She held my hand while my Tam went. Didn't say anything. Didn't need to.
You're the one she won't look at. I've been watching. Whatever you did, girl — she still knows exactly where you're standing, every second.
The wall
A cauldron of boiling bandages. Ilse's labels on every jar nearby, in the same tiny, exact handwriting you remember. One says: DO NOT. EVER. — I.M.
Shelves of empty phial-racks. Someone has counted them in chalk: 2. Then the 2 is crossed out: 1.
Shelves stacked with sunsalt phials, glowing like coals. Someone has written a new number in chalk, and underlined it twice.
The Ward Mother? In _my_ chapel? Sit, sit. I'll not take her coin. Yours, though.
A pew to sleep on and a bowl of something hot. Hundred and twenty. We used to be a chapel; now we're a mercy with a bar.
the Last Bell
I cast bells. Forty years. Every bell in this city, I could tell you its voice blindfolded.
Now I cast spoons. Spoons don't sing. But you can't eat soup with a bell, can you? Can you. I've tried.
There's a sellsword at Kiteholm loses every hand on purpose so the orphans can eat. Or he's just that bad.
Either way, I'd like to play him.
Shh. I'm bluffing. I've been bluffing for a year. About everything.
A broken pillar from the old chapel. Someone has carved a tally of every day since the Sundering. The count stopped at 300 and started over at 1, in a different hand.

src/data/maps/ch7_undercroft.js.s: Cages. Small ones — child-sized. Every door hangs open. Whatever was inside left, or was let out, or was used.

A drowned order of service, the ink run to violet: "VESPERS EVE. The Under-Choir shall descend to the Cistern and hold the Reflected Note until the Precentor's signal. Do not stop for any reason. — By order of the Hierophant."
Hymnals, swollen fat with water. One has fallen open to a page where somebody has written in the margin, very small: _I don't want to sing this one._
A reliquary statue of a Keeper holding up a lantern. Something large has rubbed against it so often that one side is polished to a shine.
A little statue of Saint Aurel, patron of tuners, still dry. Someone left a candle stub at her feet. It is not very old.
A pillar carved with a high-water mark from two hundred years ago. The water today is three hands higher.
A great bronze bell, sunk to its shoulder. Its rim is engraved: _I CALL THE LIVING. I MOURN THE DEAD. I BREAK THE LIGHTNING._ It has done none of these things in a year.
Vestry shelves. Choir robes hang in rows, dripping. There are exactly as many empty hooks as there are singers in the Loft.
A bellwright's anvil, carried all the way down here for repairs. The tools are laid out neatly, as if the smith only stepped away.

src/data/maps/ch8_kiteholm.js.s: My barge goes back down when the ember-wind turns. Which is whenever it likes.
You'll hate it up here. Then you'll never leave. Then you'll leave anyway, because that's what people like you do.
You saved my Kites. Everything's the same price, because I'm poor, but I'll _feel_ generous at you.
Scrap and Sundry! If it fell off something, I sell it. If it didn't fall off something, give it time.
Scrap-picker. I go down the ropes for metal. The Baron weighs it. The Baron's scale is a liar.
Don't go down the Underhang without rope. Don't go down with rope either. Just — don't.
Saw the Boss flying a kite up here. Laughing like a gull.
Been waiting a year to hear that. Didn't know I was waiting till I heard it.
Flew kites on the Gale Coast sixty years. Now the whole world's the sky, and I'm still flying kites.
Wind's honest. Wind doesn't promise you noon forever. It just blows.
I wash for the whole shard. Ash in everything. You get used to gray.
The Boss brings me the Kites' things once a week. Folded. He folds them. Twelve years old and he _folds_.
The Baron says he was always going to send us. He was getting his boots on. Big boots. Took a while.
Baron's terrace. Baron's air. You're breathing it, so technically you owe him.
I'm joking. Mostly. He's got a ledger for breaths.
They came, and they didn't get one. Not one Kite. My Fig is asleep in the Nest with her boots on.
Thank you. Whoever you are. Thank you.
My girl's a Kite. I'm not allowed in the Nest. Boss's rule: no grown-ups.
I'm not angry. When the raiders took Skerry's boy, nobody grown went after him. Pip did.
I saw him. On the Gallows Shard, before they cut it loose. Black armor. A mask that weeps.
He held his sword high, like a man waiting for permission. He never got it. He swung anyway.
I'm a messenger Kite. I run messages. Mostly the message is "Boss says no."
Sometimes it's "Boss says NO." That one I shout.
Aw, rats. Behind the shack was a _good_ spot.
Don't tell Tansy I was eating. I was eating.
You found me! Up here you can see the whole sky. It's mostly purple.
I like it. Don't tell Mum, she thinks purple's sad.
I was _guarding_ the skiff. Undercover. You blew my cover.
Fine. I'll go tell Tansy. She's going to be so smug.
Shhh! The Baron's terrace is the best spot. Nobody looks at the Baron's stuff. It's all ugly.
Nobody finds Sprocket. I'm Sprocket. _Nobody finds me._
I need a new spot. I need to think about my life.
The old signal mast. Someone has carved every Kite's name into it, from the bottom up. The top name is PIP. Under it, smaller, somebody else has carved: BOSS.
The town kite-pole. A hundred kite-tails flap from it, one for every child the shard has lost to the wind or the raiders. They snap in the gusts like applause.
The end of the dock. Below: nothing, then haze, then more nothing. The wind tugs at your coat like it has somewhere to show you.
The ladder down to the Underhang. The Kites have chalked a warning on the top rung: DONT. (BOSS SAYS.)
Kestrel's tab is closed, by the way. He came in, paid what he had, and ordered a water. A _water_. I nearly called Ilse.
Bed's a hammock, roof's a sail, breakfast is whatever the wind brings. Hundred and fifty.
the Rusty Anchor
Your big friend loses every hand. Every one. I used to think he was the worst card player alive.
Then I noticed he only loses when there's a Kite watching. Kites get the pot. Every time.
The Baron banned singing after the raiders' lullabies started drifting up from below.
So now I hum. Very quietly. Hmmmm. That one's about a sailor.
They say Evernoon is a city where it's always summer. They say the dead walk around in it, happy.
My wife's dead. I don't want her happy somewhere I can't go. That's selfish, isn't it. I'm drinking about it.
A hammock with a blanket folded very neatly at the foot. A greatsword leans beside it. Scratched on the wall above, a tally of days — and beside every seventh mark, a tiny drawing of a shield.
I cried when I woke up. I always cry when I wake up. Boss says it's because I'm surprised to be alive.
I think it's because waking up is sad. Even when it's good.
Bram swung his sword so hard the Baron's gun fell off the roof. Probably. I wasn't looking. I was hiding. Hiding's a job.
Rule nine: no grown-ups in the Nest.
...You're the Boss's friends? Rule nine-and-a-half: unless they're the Boss's friends. I just made that up. It's allowed.
I'm building my own kite. It's a dragon. Well. It's a triangle. It's a dragon on the inside.

A map of Kiteholm drawn on a sail, covered in pins and string. Every Kite has a pin. Every pin has a name. In the corner, a list in a careful child's hand: FOOD. WATER. SLINGSHOTS. COUNT HEADS. COUNT AGAIN.

Tucked under the map's corner: a folded scrap of paper. Inside, in pencil, a drawing of four tall people and two short ones on a beach. One of the tall ones has a sword. One of the short ones is holding her hand.
The Baron's statue is of the Baron. By the Baron. He posed for eleven days.
He says it captures his "essence." Its essence is mostly chin.
A statue of Baron Dask, welded from scrap, gazing nobly at nothing. A plaque reads: "THE AIR IS FREE. BREATHING IT IS NOT."
Crates of salvage stamped with the Choir's sunburst. The Baron does business with everyone. Everyone does business with the Baron. That is what makes him a Baron.
I bet on the Gale Roc every week. The Gale Roc has never lost.
I am very rich and very sad.
Iron Moll used to be a Dawnguard sergeant. Now she fights scrap for scrap.
She says it's the same job with better hours.
Chalked rankings: RUSTJAW. COG & SPROCKET (THE TWINS, NOT THE KITE). IRON MOLL. THE GALE ROC — UNDEFEATED. Underneath, someone has added: THE BARON (IN HIS DREAMS).

src/data/maps/ch8_underhang.js.s: A rope bridge that used to go straight down to the lower shelf. The ropes have been cut — cleanly. Someone did not want company.
A kite-tail snagged on the rocks, faded almost white. Somebody's, once.
The split prow of a Choir galleon, driven into the rock like a nail. Gilt letters on the hull, half burned away: _VIGIL_.
Wick is asleep, smiling. "...five more minutes..."
Moth is asleep. Her lips move: "...so many candles..."
A child from another shard. You don't know her name. In her sleep she is holding a hand that isn't there.
A breach in the hull. Through it: the underside of the world, and wind, and a long way down.
The captain's shelf. Hymnals, a logbook, and a child's drawing of the sun, pinned up carefully. The sun has a face. It is smiling. It is not moving.
Gloam crystals grown through the deck like teeth. They hum in the same key as the lullaby.
The lullaby swells, sweet and endless, from the bow. Somewhere in this ship, children are sleeping. Find them first.

src/data/maps/ch9_dungeons.js.s: The Marigold. A sky-ferry. Forty seats, still bolted in, all facing the windows.
On one seat, a paper bag of sweets, unopened. Someone was saving them for the view.
You climb the crane-tower. From the top, the Boneyard is a river of broken ships, running all the way down the canyon to the dark.
Far to the north-east, three bright shards hang in a slanting line, as if someone had thrown them and they never landed.
The strongbox lies open and quiet. Whatever it was, it is only a box now.
A gilded strongbox, half-buried beside the upturned hull of the Gilded Gull. The lock is shaped like a smile.
Pry it open?
The smile gets wider.
The Gilded Gull, lying on her back like a beetle. Her lift-coil housing is empty, torn open from the inside.
Luggage, still strapped to the rail. A name-tag: TILDE, AGED 9, TO AURENNE. PLEASE RETURN IF LOST.
Nobody did.
A barrel of hymnals, swollen with rain into a single block of paper. The top one is open to "Rest Ye, Dawn-Bound."
A ward of crystallized light hums around the mainmast. Up close you can hear it: the hymn, over and over, the same eight bars.
blocker:c9_benediction:ward
Crow's nest
The crow's nest has snapped off and rolled to this islet. You climb into it. From up here, through the rain, the shards wheel slowly around a single point of light.
The point of light does not wheel. It sits in the middle of everything, perfectly still.
The captain's bunk, made with corners you could cut bread with. Under the pillow: a pressed flower and a list of hymns, with "Rest Ye" underlined twice.
A crack in the rock runs all the way up through the shard. At the top, impossibly far, a sliver of sky.
Through it, every so often, the shards drift past in a slow procession — and in the middle of them all, one white point that never moves at all.
An ember crystal as tall as Bram. Inside it, very small, a shape like a bird with its wings spread, caught mid-flight.

src/data/maps/ch9_roost.js.s: Aunt Odessa says to give you the family discount. We don't have a family discount. She says to invent one.
The Ledger Exchange. Everything's for sale, and everything's written down. Aunt Odessa's rule.
I saw him shoot the line. From up here, I saw it.
Tell him— no. Don't tell him anything. Just tell him Gemma says the paint's still ugly.
He went up the plank? He actually went *up* it?
I crewed the Halcyon six years. I left when he turned east. Maybe I'll come back when he turns around.
I was his bosun, once. Best crew in the sky.
When the sea went up, we had the engines hot and the kids' island in sight. He looked at it for a long time. Then he said "east."
I got off at the first rock we came to. Haven't spoken to him since.
Stormsilk. You brought back stormsilk.
My Arlo flew a silk-rigger. Could I— no. No, it's for your ship. Just let me look at it a moment.
...Thank you. It still smells of weather.
I knit with sailcloth. It's all that falls out of the sky now — sails, and the people who were under them.
My Arlo went up the morning the sun broke. I keep knitting him scarves. I've got eleven. He'll be ever so warm.
The Noon Spire. Of course it was the Spire.
I sang in the Choir for twenty years. There is nothing I want to say to the Hierophant that a hymn would carry.
I was a Cantor of the Choir. I took off the robe the night the sun broke. Kept the hood. It's cold.
Pilgrims still fly north, you know. To a white tower on the brightest shard. They say inside it is always the afternoon of a summer festival, and the dead are there, waiting.
They say a great many things. The pilgrims don't come back to say otherwise.
Bird stew! Bird stew! Don't ask what bird. I don't ask the birds what you are.
There used to be seagulls, you know. Before. I miss complaining about them.
We came from the Mirefen shards. Walked the sky-bridges, three weeks.
Nia sleeps fine now. I don't. Somebody has to listen for the bridges creaking.
You're going to try. You said. I heard you.
Are you the girl from the song? The one with the red hair?
Did you really break the sun?
Yes. I did.
Can you fix it?
I'm going to try.
The song doesn't say that part. Somebody should put it in.
Lift's yours, with Mags's key. Mind the bottom — it bites.
Not the lift. The Boneyard. The lift's very well behaved.
Lift's chained. Mags keeps the key. Mags keeps everything.
Down there's the Boneyard. Everything that fell out of the sky. Some of it's still moving.
The skiff
An empty mooring post. The cut line trails over the edge into nothing.
Corvin's skiff: a one-man sky-boat, sleek and patched, moored to the Lip by a single line.
Its tank is full. Someone has been keeping it full.
The bow
Ash, and the long scar in it where a ship used to lie.
HALCYON, in chipped gold leaf. Below it, smaller, an older name has been painted over. You can just make out the first letters: H-A-L.
A campfire of kite-sticks and chair legs. Someone has drawn a ship in the ash beside it, with a very large flag and a very small captain.
A table made from a door. The chart on it is mostly blank, with careful notes in the margins: HERE BE NOTHING. HERE TOO. HERE, POSSIBLY, SOUP.
Kite-tails and prayer-flags snap on the lines. Someone has stitched names onto them. Dozens of names. Under the newest: COME HOME.
Ox's anvil, scattered with clock-hands. Dozens of them, all pointing different ways.
The lift winch. A chalk tally on its housing counts the people who went down to the Boneyard this year. A second tally counts the ones who came up. The second one is shorter.
The stocks. Someone has carved, very small, into the wood: THE GOAT WAS A DOG.
Lift's chained. Mags has the key.
Not yet. We came here for a ship.
You... got a coil. Out of the Boneyard.
...Go show Mags. She'll be insufferable. Let her.
Mags. Wreck. Up the canyon. I'm not coming.
Don't look at me like that, sparrow. Your mother used to look at me like that.
Beds upstairs. Two hundred. The Captain's old room's free — first time in a year he isn't sleeping on my bar.
Beds upstairs, two hundred a night. Breakfast is whatever Marta caught. Don't ask what.
the Last Call
Zzz... five more minutes...
...five more years...
Bottles, labeled in Tuck's square hand: NOT FOR CORVIN. One new label, the ink still wet: STILL NOT FOR CORVIN. GOOD.
Bottles, mostly empty, all labeled in Tuck's square hand: NOT FOR CORVIN.
A card table. The felt is worn through in exactly one place: where the dealer's left hand rests.
Debits on the left, credits on the right. Debtors on the carpet.
Madam Quill has never once been wrong about a number. She's been wrong about people. Twice. She keeps a ledger of that too.
Ledgers to the ceiling, each spine labeled with a year. The newest are labeled only: AFTER.
A ledger lies open to a page near the back. There is a tidy gap where one page was torn out.
A ledger lies open to a page near the back, worn soft with handling. ASHE, C. The column of figures runs to the bottom and over the page.
A small statue of a woman holding scales. Someone has balanced a coin on each pan. They are perfectly level.

src/data/maps/lanternfall.js.s:
LANTERNFALL — Westmost Light of Solmere.
The Kindling: tomorrow at noon, at the Lantern.
They say the Hierophant hasn't left Aurenne in eleven years. And he's coming _here_. For _our_ children.
I've swept my step four times.
You got VANGUARD? That's the best one! Can I hold your sword? Can I? Just the handle?
Are you getting your Crest tomorrow? I hope I get Vanguard when I'm sixteen. Or Arcanist. Something with explosions.
One Crest, one life, girl. My father was a Warden, I'm a Warden, my boy's a Warden.
The light knows what you are. No sense arguing with the light.
My Tamsy got Mender last spring. Cried for a week — she wanted Cantor.
She's good at it now, though. Funny how the light knows.
That white ship's got sails like an angel's wings. Never seen the like.
Nor such a quiet crew.
Tide's out further than I've ever seen. You can walk to the eel rocks.
The sea's waiting for something.
Any minute now! The Hierophant's ship! I've been here since dawn.
If you see white sails, scream. I will too. We'll scream together.
Tobias says the net's with Brisa. Tobias says a lot of things.
Good luck tomorrow, love. Whatever the light says, you're still our Wren.
The village well. Someone has carved WREN + ILSE + THE SEA into the stone. You remember carving it.
Your mother's herb garden. Rosemary, thyme, and a sea-lavender that has never once flowered.
No time for the caves now.
Not in this storm.
The tide caves... Mom would kill me. I should do my chores first.

src/data/maps/lanternfall_interiors.js.s: Your father's books. Sea charts, star charts, a novel about a pirate queen with the last chapter torn out.
A shelf of your own books. Every one has washed ashore at some point. Most of them are still a little salty.
Two plates. There have been two plates for seven years.
Nana's been up since four, stewing kelp for tomorrow. The whole house smells like a tide pool.
Jars of dried herbs, labeled in Ilse's tiny, exact handwriting. One just says: DO NOT. LET WREN. TOUCH.
A cauldron of something green. It smells, generously, like the sea.
A bed and a bowl of chowder, love? Ten gold.
—and THEN I said, "Not today, Gloam-beast!" and I— oh! Wren. Ilse. Hello.
I was just telling these children about my many heroic deeds. All true. Mostly true. True in spirit.
Big day tomorrow! Don't worry about the Kindling. The light's never wrong. Mine said Warden and look at me. ...Don't look too closely.
Bram says he fought a Gloam-beast with a spoon!
Came in from Port Gale last week. Mainland's jumpy. Talk of shadows in the Whisperwold. Lights going out in villages.
Folk say the Lanterns are getting tired. Like old men.
Tonics, charms, a sword or two. Kindling special: everything's the same price as always.
A crate of salted fish and a note: "MAELA — DON'T." Below it, in different handwriting: "I DID."

src/data/maps/lf_dungeons.js.s: The great lamp of Lanternfall. Inside the glass, something like a small sun sleeps in a bed of brass.
The Dawnstone. Warm as a hand.
Empty. Mom and the Hierophant must be up in the lamp room. She said home — and I'm asleep on my feet. Bed first.

Tip — Monsters roam the caves, and HP doesn't recover between battles. Use *Tonics* from the menu, and rest at the golden *Hearthstone* deeper in. If a fight turns against you, *Flee* (each try is likelier to work). Entering a new area autosaves.
A violet crystal, half-sunk in the rock. It is cold enough to hurt. You get the feeling it is listening.
Keep your weight low. She bucks in a swell.

src/data/maps/postgame_abyss.js.s: Where someone sat down to rest
Where a child drew in chalk
Where a city fell out of the books
Where the saints lost their faces
Where the wolves have no prey
Where a queen ruled no one
Where colours were not yet invented
Where the first tree stood alone
A lamp hangs from a chain that goes up and up into the dark. The lift will not come down while the warden of this stair still stands.
A small patch of dusk, curled up on the marble. It is breathing, slowly. It is asleep.

src/data/maps/postgame_gate.js.s:
THE NADIR LIGHT — the Eighth Lantern.
Underkeeper: O. Vey.
Mind the edge. The edge does not mind you.

THE ECHO COLOSSEUM
Proprietor: D. Marlow, late of Kiteholm.
Fights nightly. (It is always night.)
The great lamp turns slowly, throwing its beam not out to sea but straight down into the rift.
Somewhere far below, something that has never had a shape turns its face away from the light, and sleeps on.
Steps cut into the cliff, going down into a dark so thick it looks wet. Someone has scratched beside them: 30 FLIGHTS. NO RAIL.

RANKS I–X. ONE MEMORY EACH.
Prizes for first victories only.
The management is not responsible for anything you remember.
(It cheers, a beat after everyone else, for a fight that happened years ago.)
(It is booing someone. You check. It is booing you. It is the memory of someone who lost money on you.)
(It mouths a name, over and over. Not yours. Not anyone's anymore.)
